Good products often require people to put together very janky, messy, and hacky technical solutions together that WILL take one or more people to just maintain full time. This is also why experienced senior engineers are worth their weight in gold. 

Simple, clean, mature applications and abstractions can be built by anybody. But modeling the real world is incredibly messy. Killing all technical debt, as noble as it can seem, is often not the best use of time and finite engineering power. Experienced engineers are the people who can look at the real world pains and then come up with a reasonably architected model. And that architectural intuition often comes from pain: you only know which battles to pick by fighting them.

When I was 17, I applied to 26 universities in the United States. I got rejected by 20, waitlisted by 3, and admitted by 3. My best offer, which to this day I am still grateful for, was UIUC.

I looked at the UIUC curriculum and found out I could speedrun the class and finish my undergrad in just four semesters. I used my AP/IB credits, overloaded some semesters, tested out of some, took summer classes, transferred general education classes from community college, and decided to go to EPFL in August 2022 to finish my last semester of undergrad there. I graduated from UIUC at 19 in May 2023. 

I did this partially to save on the tuition my parents have to pay. But also because I don’t want to put off life experiences. Even if I enjoyed school, and student life, if not I wouldn’t have finished my master’s at 21 two years later, I didn’t want to spend immense amounts of time stuck in the same intro classes where I already know the knowledge. I think, with a little bit of planning and ingenuity, you don’t have to put a pause on valuable life experiences, such as solo travel while I was abroad in Switzerland at EPFL. 

Here were some of my EPFL “integration week” photos around mid-September 2022, a week and a half before school started.

At a certain point and scale, coding evolves from putting together an application with a certain set of features to building systems. You will need to build systems if you 

- want your application to run quickly, smoothly, reliably at a large number of users,
- ever need interaction between users,
- don’t want to waste huge amounts of money and hardware capacity

Systems are not an easy discipline. Good system engineering requires an understanding of multiple different academic disciplines:

- algorithms
- distributed systems
- hardware

Each one of these disciplines will take months to years to learn and master. And this is not even considering putting it into practice. Good systems engineers need to:

- know how to architect clean systems, 
- juggle customer requirements and evolving specifications with good engineering practices,
- and work on existing real world systems. And real world systems, including systems at incredibly valuable companies, are incredibly messy! You need to know what technical debt battles are worth fighting and refactoring, and which ones to NOT touch. If you need an example, just look at Claude Code’s leaked harness code. 

Knowing how to do each one of these above will take huge amounts of time. Big companies, while they absolutely have the money for system talent, finding such talent is not as easy as “just throw money at the problem”. The number of good systems engineers in the world is quite limited. A lot of smart people that I know are not that interested in systems. They are more interested in ML, compilers, pure theoretical CS, and don’t want to deal with the messy worldly nature of systems. xAI would have loved to been able to use more than 11% of their compute capacity before renting all of their compute capacity out to Anthropic. 

That’s why devtool + infra companies that abstract hard systems work away from you (AWS, Vercel, Databricks) make ridiculous amounts of money, despite having problems. AWS is not that developer friendly. Vercel has had reliability issues with deployment in the past. Databricks has had a reputation for being a place where customers set money on fire. There are just very few companies and people who can actually do the work of handling systems. 

And systems are not just one singular discipline. They branch into many different niches, like ML systems. For each one of these systems companies, they are indisputably the king of their niche. And that’s how they have so much pricing power, because many companies can’t and won’t try to find systems engineers who can build these systems from scratch on bare metal.

When you start working in industry, you will quickly learn that technical debt is something where you pick your fights carefully. 

The gold standard for any system is 100% correctness and rigor, where you can back every single line of code with formal mathematical reasoning. 

But you need to ship fast and increasingly have the pressure of AI coding agents on you. You realize you can’t let perfection be the enemy of good. 

So, instead, you need clean mental models of the most critical systems and components that you touch. Core components have to work pretty much all the time. The others, you slowly iterate, refactor and improve upon.
